fields.Front: What does 'three nines' (99.9%) availability translate to in downtime per year?
fields.Back: About 8.76 hours of downtime per year.

fields.Front: What does 'five nines' (99.999%) availability translate to in downtime per year?
fields.Back: About 5.26 minutes of downtime per year.

fields.Front: Why is an SLO typically set stricter than the corresponding SLA?
fields.Back: To leave a safety margin, so the team notices and fixes problems internally before the customer-facing SLA is actually breached.

fields.Front: What is redundancy in system design?
fields.Back: Running duplicate components (servers, replicas, data centers) so that if one fails, others can take over without a service outage.
The automatic process of switching to a redundant/standby component when the active one fails.
Under failure or overload, a system keeps its core functionality working by disabling or simplifying non-essential features rather than failing completely.

fields.Front: What problem does a circuit breaker solve?
fields.Back: It stops a service from repeatedly calling a downstream dependency that is failing, failing fast instead and giving the dependency time to recover.

fields.Front: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
fields.Back: Closed (calls flow normally), Open (calls fail immediately without trying), and Half-Open (a few test calls are let through to check for recovery).

fields.Front: Why use exponential backoff when retrying a failed request?
fields.Back: Increasing the wait time between retries avoids overwhelming an already struggling downstream service with a retry storm.

fields.Front: Why should retry backoff usually include random jitter?
fields.Back: Without jitter, many clients retry at the exact same intervals in sync, causing repeated synchronized traffic spikes (a 'thundering herd').

fields.Front: What does a request timeout protect against?
fields.Back: A slow or unresponsive dependency holding a caller's resources (threads/connections) indefinitely, which could cascade into resource exhaustion.
Isolating resources (e.g. thread pools or connection pools) per dependency or service, so one failing dependency can't exhaust resources needed by others.

fields.Front: How does the token bucket rate-limiting algorithm work?
fields.Back: Tokens are added to a bucket at a fixed rate up to a max capacity; each request consumes a token, and requests are rejected/delayed once the bucket is empty — this allows short bursts.

fields.Front: How does the leaky bucket rate-limiting algorithm work?
fields.Back: Requests enter a fixed-size queue and are processed ('leak out') at a constant rate, smoothing bursty traffic into a steady output rate.

fields.Front: What is an idempotency key used for in an API?
fields.Back: A client-supplied unique id attached to a request so that if the request is retried (e.g. after a timeout), the server can detect the duplicate and avoid double-processing it (e.g. double-charging a payment).

fields.Front: In back-of-envelope estimation, how do you roughly estimate QPS from daily active users?
fields.Back: (daily active users × actions per user per day) / 86,400 seconds, often multiplied by a peak-factor (e.g. 2-3x) to get peak QPS. Note: a day has about 86,400 seconds (~10^5), a useful constant to memorize.

fields.Front: What is the difference between a liveness and a readiness health check?
fields.Back: Liveness asks 'is the process still running/not deadlocked' (restart it if failing); readiness asks 'is the service ready to accept traffic' (remove it from the load balancer if failing, without necessarily restarting it).

fields.Front: Why is monitoring with alerting important beyond just logging?
fields.Back: Logs require someone to go look; monitoring with alerts proactively notifies the team when a metric crosses a threshold, enabling faster incident response.

fields.Text: {{c1::SLA}} (Service Level Agreement) is the external contract/promise made to customers; {{c2::SLO}} (Service Level Objective) is the internal target a team aims for; {{c3::SLI}} (Service Level Indicator) is the actual measured metric.
Token bucket allows {{c1::bursts}} of traffic up to the bucket size, while leaky bucket enforces a {{c2::constant, smoothed}} output rate regardless of burstiness.
Rough powers-of-two/ten memory sizes for estimation: {{c1::1 KB}} ≈ 10^3 bytes, {{c2::1 MB}} ≈ 10^6 bytes, {{c3::1 GB}} ≈ 10^9 bytes, {{c4::1 TB}} ≈ 10^12 bytes.

Latency numbers worth memorizing: L1 cache reference ≈ 1 ns, main memory reference ≈ 100 ns, round trip within the same data center ≈ 0.5 ms, and a round trip {{c1::across the US/continent}} ≈ tens of ms (roughly 40-60 ms).
